title: Embodied learning using a tangible user interface: The effects of haptic perception and selective pointing on a spatial learning task
research_question: To investigate whether additional haptic input (via a tangible user interface) and interactive label presentation (selective pointing vs. permanent display) are beneficial when learning with 3D objects, specifically heart anatomy.

participants.description: University students (Mage = 23.9 years, SDage = 3.43; 65 female, 31 male) predominantly in Media Communication and Psychology at a German university. 94 native German speakers. 84 right-handed, 9 ambilateral, 3 left-handed. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Excluded those with recent heart anatomy learning or dyslexia.
participants.recruitment: Received course credit or 6 € for participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A 3D model of a human heart with 21 floating labels. Interacted with either a standard computer mouse or a Tangible User Interface (TUI). The TUI was a life-size plastic heart model (200g) with a motion sensor and a stylus pen.

measures.instrument: Multiple choice test (5 questions) and oral interview
Visual retention test (labeling 3D heart model from front and back side, 31 items)
Three transfer tasks (two cross-sections of 3D model, heart CT scan labeling, 22 items total)
Cognitive load questionnaire (Eysink et al., 2009) with scales for intrinsic, extraneous, germane, and overall load (9-point scale, 6 items for agreement, 3 for extraneous load)
QSM/FAM questionnaire (Rheinberg et al., 2001) with scales for 'interest', 'efficacy', and 'challenge' (7-point scale, 13 items)
AttrakDiff questionnaire (Hassenzahl et al., 2003) with scales for 'hedonic quality - stimulation' and 'pragmatic quality' (7-point scale, 15 items)

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse)
findings.mechanism: Holding and touching a complex 3D object facilitates the formation of a coherent spatial representation, providing a persistent guide for orientation and integrating visual/verbal information.
findings.quote: Retention performance was higher when the TUI was used instead of the mouse

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.mechanism: The effect of label display mode is different for the two input devices: selective pointing is better for mouse, permanent display is better for TUI.
findings.quote: significant interaction between input device and label display mode [F(1, 92) = 6.78, p = .011, η = .06]

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.quote: the transfer task (...) yielded no significant differences in a 2 × 2 ANOVA (...) all ps ≥ .555

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.quote: no significant effect regarding intrinsic load (all ps ≥ .129)

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse)
findings.mechanism: Additional haptic input from holding the plastic model acts as a comprehension aid, providing a stable reference frame and reducing mental effort for spatial representation, thus lowering germane load.
findings.quote: Using the TUI resulted in a lower germane load (...) with a significant main effect of input device, F(1, 92) = 8.08, p = .006, η = .08.

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.mechanism: Permanent display increases extraneous load with mouse, but lowers it with TUI. Selective display of information in pointing condition may give participants the impression that the learning task is less demanding for mouse users.
findings.quote: significant interactions between input device and label display mode (...) F(1, 92) = 4.11, p = .046, np = .04

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.mechanism: Permanent display increases overall load with mouse, but lowers it with TUI. Selective display of information in pointing condition may give participants the impression that the learning task is less demanding for mouse users.
findings.quote: significant interactions between input device and label display mode (...) F(1, 92) = 4.79, p = .031, np = .05

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse)
findings.mechanism: The dynamic and natural experience of manipulating a virtual 3D object with a tangible physical object generates interest.
findings.quote: main effect of the factor input device on interest [F(1, 91 ) = 6, p = .016, np = .06], indicating that the TUI led to an increased interest

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.mechanism: Selective pointing promoted efficacy for mouse users but was detrimental for TUI users due to motor coordination necessary with the pen.
findings.quote: interaction between input device and label display mode, F(1, 92) = 4.17, p = .044, nẞ = .04. This result shows that the selective pointing feature promoted a feeling of efficacy for mouse users, while this feature was detrimental for efficacy in the TUI condition.

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse) AND Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.quote: No effect was found on the scale challenge (all ps ≥ .54).

findings.antecedent: Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
findings.mechanism: Selective pointing mode was preferred, regardless of input device.
findings.quote: main effect of selective pointing on the scale “hedonic quality – stimulation” [F(1, 91) = 7.78, p = .006, η = .08], indicating a preference for the selective pointing mode

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse)
findings.mechanism: TUI offers a multi-sensory user experience perceived as better suited for the learning task.
findings.quote: main effect of input device on “pragmatic quality” [F(1, 92) = 7.72, p = .007, np = .08] in favor of the TUI.

mechanisms: Multimodal perceptual input (haptic feedback from TUI) facilitates the formation of coherent spatial representations by providing a persistent guide for orientation and integrating visual/verbal information, thereby lowering germane cognitive load.

Selective pointing for mouse users reduces distractive visual influences and frees up cognitive capacity by focusing attention on one area, potentially promoting systematic learning strategies and self-cueing, leading to lower extraneous and overall cognitive load.

For TUI users, the additional motor coordination required by selective pointing with a stylus pen imposes a high toll on attentional resources and working memory, outweighing any benefits and leading to lower learning performance and self-efficacy.
The TUI's dynamic and natural manipulation of a virtual 3D object generates increased interest and is perceived as more practical due to its multi-sensory experience.
moderators: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs. Mouse)
Label display mode (Selective Pointing vs. Permanent Display)
implementation_implications: TUIs are advantageous for learning relatively complex objects that are small enough to be held in one hand, leading to better learning outcomes, lower cognitive load, and increased interest and perceived practicality.
For mouse interfaces, selective pointing (hiding unactivated labels) can improve learning performance and reduce cognitive load by reducing visual clutter and promoting focused attention.
For TUI interfaces, permanent display of all labels is preferable to selective pointing, as the motor coordination required for precise pointing with a stylus can be detrimental to learning.

Designers should carefully consider the costs (e.g., motor coordination, complexity) and benefits (e.g., multimodal input, externalization, epistemic actions) of interactive features, rather than assuming high interactivity is always beneficial.

Perceived usability ratings (e.g., hedonic quality) may not always align with actual cognitive load or learning performance, suggesting that cognitive load assessments might be better predictors of learning outcomes.

limitations: The transfer task may have been too difficult for participants without prior medical training, or too cognitively challenging for the short learning time.
The TUI's benefits might not extend to cognitively challenging tasks like labeling cross-sections.
The position of the virtual heart could not be changed in mouse conditions, which might limit generalizability.
The study did not investigate whether single-handed 3D pointing devices offer comparable positive effects to mouse pointing.
The novelty effect of the TUI might have contributed to increased interest, which could wear off with widespread use.
